s: The Great Granary, described as the largest building of the city, has been found at which Harappan site?
x: The Great Granary, regarded as the largest building at the site, was found at Mohenjodaro.
tq: Use the site–structure association directly.
sec: Granaries → site and structure type

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Mohenjodaro — Great Granary
2. Harappa — Two rows of six granaries
3. Lothal — Warehouse on a raised platform beside the dock
4. Rakhigarhi — Reported granary
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Mohenjodaro had the Great Granary, Harappa had two rows of six granaries, Lothal had a raised warehouse near the dock, and a granary has also been reported at Rakhigarhi.
tq: Check each site–structure pair before selecting the combined code.
sec: Granaries → site and structure type

s:
At Harappa, the granaries were characterised by which of the following features?
1. Two rows of six granaries each
2. Proximity to the river
3. Circular working platforms
4. Single-roomed barracks
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Harappa had two rows of six granaries each near the river, together with circular working platforms and single-roomed barracks.
tq: Identify the option containing the complete set of associated features.
sec: Granaries → site and structure type

s: Which one of the following statements regarding the interpretation of Harappan granaries is correct?
o: They were constructed only for residential purposes.
They were exclusively used as temples.
They are generally read as stores of farm surplus, though the interpretation is debated.
They are universally accepted as royal palaces.
x: Granaries are commonly interpreted as storage places for agricultural surplus, but this interpretation remains debated.
tq: Distinguish a prevailing interpretation from an absolute conclusion.
sec: Granaries → site and structure type

s: The warehouse on a raised platform beside the dock is associated with which site?
x: Lothal had a warehouse on a raised platform beside the dock; seal impressions were also associated with the warehouse.
tq: Match the distinctive structure with its site.
sec: Granaries → site and structure type

s: Which one of the following was a hallmark of Harappan town planning?
o: Settlements without drainage or public buildings
Grid-patterned streets and organised civic divisions
Irregular streets centred on royal palaces
x: Organised town planning, including grid-patterned streets and civic divisions, is a hallmark of the Indus Valley Civilization.
tq: Recognise the broad civilisational feature rather than a minor detail.
sec: Town planning hallmarks - grid, orientation, divisions

s:
Consider the following statements about the street plan of Harappan cities:
1. Streets generally ran north–south and east–west.
2. The streets crossed one another at right angles.
3. The streets divided the city into blocks.
4. Main streets were about 30 feet or approximately 10 metres wide.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The Harappan grid plan consisted of north–south and east–west streets crossing at right angles, dividing cities into blocks; main streets were about 30 feet or 10 metres wide.
tq: Test orientation, geometry and measurement together.
sec: Town planning hallmarks - grid, orientation, divisions

s: Which Harappan site is associated with the earliest street layout mentioned in the context of Indus town planning?
x: Mohenjodaro shows the first street layout referred to in the context of Harappan town planning.
tq: Use the site-specific chronological association.
sec: Town planning hallmarks - grid, orientation, divisions

s: With reference to the division of Harappan cities, which one of the following is correct?
o: The citadel was a raised and fortified western area, while the lower town lay to the east.
The lower town was always situated on a higher platform than the citadel.
The citadel was generally on the eastern side and the lower town on the western side.
Both the citadel and lower town were exclusively residential areas.
x: The western citadel stood on a raised, fortified platform and contained public buildings, while the eastern lower town was associated with commoners’ houses.
tq: Check the direction and functional contrast between the two urban divisions.
sec: Town planning hallmarks - grid, orientation, divisions

s: Which of the following categories correctly represents the three types of Harappan buildings?
o: Residential houses, larger buildings and public buildings
x: Harappan buildings are classified into residential houses, larger buildings and public buildings. No temples have been found in the civilization as stated.
tq: Recall the exact classification and avoid substituting familiar ancient building types.
sec: Town planning hallmarks - grid, orientation, divisions

s: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct regarding Harappan town planning?
o: The cities displayed a grid pattern.
Public buildings were generally associated with the citadel.
The same size of brick was used for every construction.
The main streets were approximately 10 metres wide.
x: Brick sizes differed according to construction. House bricks measured about 7 × 14 × 28 cm, while city-wall bricks measured about 10 × 20 × 40 cm, though both followed the same ratio.
tq: Find the overgeneralised statement using the exception in brick dimensions.
sec: Town planning hallmarks - grid, orientation, divisions

s: Which one of the following sites had three urban divisions consisting of a citadel, a middle town and a lower town?
x: Dholavira was divided into a citadel, a middle town and a lower town; the citadel itself included a castle and bailey.
tq: Identify the site with the exceptional three-part plan.

s: Which Harappan site is noted for having no citadel?
x: Chanhudaro is noted as the only city in the listed comparison without a citadel.

s:
Consider the following pairs:
a. Mohenjodaro — Citadel and lower town
a. Harappa — Citadel and lower town
b. Kalibangan — Citadel and fortified lower town
c. Lothal — Citadel and lower town in one enclosure
d. Sutkagendor — Citadel and lower city
Which of the above pairs are correctly matched?
x: All the listed site–plan associations are correct. Kalibangan had a fortified lower town, Lothal had both divisions in one enclosure, and Sutkagendor had a citadel and lower city.
tq: Start with the distinctive exceptions and verify the remaining standard pairs.

s: Which one of the following sites is correctly matched with its distinctive town-planning feature?
o: Chanhudaro — Three-part city with a middle town
Lothal — Citadel and lower town in separate distant enclosures
Banawali — Radial streets and no systematic drainage
x: Banawali is noted for radial streets, the only such site in the comparison, and for lacking systematic drainage. Dholavira had three parts, Chanhudaro had no citadel, and Lothal had both divisions in one enclosure.

s: The standard proportion of Harappan bricks was generally expressed as:

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Harappan bricks:
1. Burnt bricks were the common building material.
2. Mud bricks were used for fillings and platforms.
3. Mud bricks were also used at Kalibangan.
4. Dholavira used sandstone and limestone blocks as an exception.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Burnt bricks were common, while mud bricks were used for fillings, platforms and at Kalibangan. Dholavira was an exception where sandstone and limestone blocks were used.
tq: Combine the general rule with the stated material exceptions.

s: Which one of the following correctly gives the brick dimensions used for houses and city walls respectively?
x: House bricks measured about 7 × 14 × 28 cm and city-wall bricks about 10 × 20 × 40 cm. Their sizes differed, but both followed the 1:2:4 ratio.
tq: Compare paired measurements rather than relying only on the common ratio.

s: The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro was located:
o: Beside the dockyard in the lower town
Inside a residential courtyard at Harappa
On the fortified lower town of Kalibangan
x: The Great Bath was situated on the citadel mound of Mohenjodaro.
tq: Link the monument to both its site and urban division.

s: The approximate dimensions and depth of the Great Bath at Mohenjodaro were:

s: Which combination of materials was used in the construction and waterproofing of the Great Bath?
o: Burnt bricks, gypsum mortar and bitumen
Mud bricks, lime plaster and clay coating
Limestone, mud mortar and natural resin
x: The Great Bath was built with burnt bricks set in gypsum mortar and was waterproofed with a layer of bitumen.
tq: Distinguish construction material from the waterproofing agent.

s: Which one of the following statements about the Great Bath is correct?
o: It had flights of steps at its northern and southern ends and is generally interpreted as a place for ritual bathing and purification.
It was situated in the lower town and served only as a grain store.
It had no steps and was used exclusively for irrigation.
It had flights of steps at its eastern and western ends and was certainly a royal palace.
x: The Great Bath had flights of steps at its north and south ends. It is most commonly interpreted as a place for ritual bathing and purification, although a public water tank interpretation also exists.
tq: Combine structural details with the cautious interpretation of purpose.

s: A Harappan house with rooms arranged around an open central space, bathrooms connected to drains and staircases leading upward would most likely indicate:

Doors and windows generally opened onto the main streets for public visibility.
Bathrooms were built without floors and were disconnected from drainage channels.
All houses were identical in size and layout.

House drains → street drains → soak pits or main channels
Main channels → street drains → house drains → soak pits
Street drains → house drains → soak pits → main channels

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Indus Valley drainage systems:

2. Manholes were provided for cleaning.

4. Streets were designed with a slope to facilitate natural flow.

s: Which one of the following statements about drainage in smaller Indus Valley settlements is correct?
o: Planned drainage was confined to the largest cities.
Kalibangan had wooden drains, whereas Banawali lacked a systematic drainage system.
Banawali had the most elaborate drainage system and Kalibangan had none.
Both Kalibangan and Banawali used only stone drains.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Indus Valley and contemporary West Asian civilizations:
1. No palaces or temples have been clearly identified in the Indus Valley cities.
2. Indus Valley drainage was more advanced than that of contemporary Mesopotamia and Egypt.
